topic: Physics — Changes of state and the particle model
subject: combined-science

items.q: Which of these is the definition of the density of a material?
items.correct: The mass of the sample divided by its volume.
items.misconception: The volume the sample fills divided by its own mass.
items.why: Students remember that the equation contains a division but not its direction, and arithmetic habits push them to divide the larger value by the smaller one so the answer is greater than one. Use the unit as the check. Density is quoted in kg/m^3, and the slash tells you kilograms are divided by metres cubed, so mass has to be on top.
items.random_wrong: The mass of the sample multiplied by the volume.

items.q: In the equation ρ = m/V, what do the symbols m and V stand for?
items.correct: m stands for mass and V stands for volume.
items.misconception: m stands for metres and V stands for volume.
items.why: The same letters are used for other quantities elsewhere in the course, and m is also the abbreviation for the metre, so a student who has learned symbols by their commonest meaning misreads the equation. Read the symbols back from the specification's own list of quantities and units for this equation, and check the result: mass over volume gives kg/m^3, which is the unit of density.
items.random_wrong: m stands for mass and V is the speed it moves.

items.q: Which unit does the specification use for density?
items.correct: kilograms per metre cubed, written kg/m³
items.misconception: kilograms times metres cubed, kg m³
items.why: Multiplying is the default operation when a student can recall which two quantities are involved but not the relationship. It also matches a vague feeling that bigger means denser. Test any suggested version against the unit. Multiplying kilograms by metres cubed gives kg m^3, which is not the unit of density; dividing gives kg/m^3, which is.
items.random_wrong: kilograms per metre squared, kg/m²

items.q: A cube of steel has sides of 0.10 m and a mass of 7.8 kg. What is its density?
items.correct: 7800 kg/m³
items.why: Multiplying is the default operation when a student can recall which two quantities are involved but not the relationship. It also matches a vague feeling that bigger means denser. Test any suggested version against the unit. Multiplying kilograms by metres cubed gives kg m^3, which is not the unit of density; dividing gives kg/m^3, which is.
items.random_wrong: 780 kg/m³

items.q: A liquid has a density of 800 kg/m³. What volume is occupied by 2.0 kg of the liquid?
items.why: Mass and weight are used interchangeably in everyday language, and both are met in the same part of the course, so a student happily converts a balance reading into newtons and uses that instead. Keep the two apart by unit. The density equation takes kilograms; newtons are a force. A balance measures mass, so its reading only needs converting from grams to kilograms.

items.q: Aluminium has a density of 2.7 g/cm³. What is this density in kg/m³?
items.correct: 2700 kg/m³
items.why: The student notices only the mass part of the unit and applies the g to kg conversion, forgetting that the volume unit has changed as well and by a much larger factor. Convert the two parts separately: 1 g becomes 0.001 kg, and 1 cm^3 becomes 0.000001 m^3. Dividing 0.001 by 0.000001 gives 1000, so multiply by 1000. Water at 1.0 g/cm^3 is 1000 kg/m^3, which is a useful check.
items.random_wrong: 2.7 kg/m³

items.q: A rectangular block measures 0.30 m by 0.20 m by 0.10 m. What is its volume?
items.why: Adding is easier than multiplying three decimals, and the student is not checking the unit of the answer. The idea that volume is a product of three lengths has been learned as a rule rather than understood. Check the unit produced by the operation. Adding metres to metres gives metres, not metres cubed. Only multiplying three lengths gives m^3.
items.random_wrong: 0.6 m³

items.q: A balance shows the mass of a block as 250 g. Which value should be used for m to obtain a density in kg/m³?
items.correct: 0.25 kg, the reading divided by 1000
items.misconception: 250 000 kg, the reading multiplied by 1000
items.why: The student notices only the mass part of the unit and applies the g to kg conversion, forgetting that the volume unit has changed as well and by a much larger factor. Convert the two parts separately: 1 g becomes 0.001 kg, and 1 cm^3 becomes 0.000001 m^3. Dividing 0.001 by 0.000001 gives 1000, so multiply by 1000. Water at 1.0 g/cm^3 is 1000 kg/m^3, which is a useful check.
items.random_wrong: 250 kg, the balance reading itself

items.q: A solid aluminium bar is cut exactly in half. What is the density of each half?
items.correct: The same as the whole bar, because mass and volume both halve.
items.misconception: Half the original value, since each piece has half the mass.
items.why: Density is treated as a quantity that an object owns, like mass, rather than as a ratio. Since mass obviously halves, density is assumed to halve with it. Write the calculation out for both halves and show that the answer is identical. Reinforce that density is a property of the material, so every piece of the same material has the same value.
items.random_wrong: A quarter of the original value, since mass times volume is used.

items.q: Which statement describes the arrangement of particles in a solid, a liquid and a gas?
items.correct: Solid: regular and touching; liquid: random but touching; gas: random and far apart.
items.misconception: Solid: regular and touching; liquid: evenly spaced out; gas: far apart.
items.why: The order solid, liquid, gas suggests an evenly spaced sequence, and many textbook diagrams exaggerate the gaps in a liquid to show that its particles can move. Compare real densities: liquid water is 1000 kg/m^3 and ice is about 920 kg/m^3, while steam is well under 1 kg/m^3. Liquids sit next to solids, nowhere near gases.
items.random_wrong: Solid: small particles; liquid: larger ones; gas: the largest of all.

items.q: A student is drawing simple particle diagrams. Which drawing models a liquid correctly?
items.correct: Circles of one size touching, with no pattern.
items.misconception: Circles of one size in a neat grid, evenly spaced.
items.why: Students are taught that a solid is regular and draw a grid for tidiness, spacing the circles out so the arrangement is visible. The gaps are a drawing convenience that then gets read as physics. Judge a diagram on two separate features: the arrangement, regular or random, and the spacing, touching or far apart. A solid must be regular and touching.
items.random_wrong: Circles drawn larger than those in the solid diagram.

items.q: Why is the density of steam so much lower than the density of liquid water?
items.correct: Its molecules are much further apart, so that mass fills more space.
items.misconception: Its molecules are lighter and smaller than those in the liquid water, too.
items.why: Gases feel weightless, so their particles are imagined to be lighter. The student is changing the mass of a particle to explain a change that is actually caused by spacing. Insist that steam is made of exactly the same molecules as the water it came from. Nothing about a molecule changes on boiling except how far it is from its neighbours.
items.random_wrong: Some of the water's mass is destroyed when the liquid is boiled away.

items.q: Ice floats on liquid water. What does this show about ice, and why?
items.correct: It is less dense, because its molecules are held slightly further apart.
items.misconception: It is denser, because the solid state of a substance is always the denser one.
items.why: The order solid, liquid, gas suggests an evenly spaced sequence, and many textbook diagrams exaggerate the gaps in a liquid to show that its particles can move. Compare real densities: liquid water is 1000 kg/m^3 and ice is about 920 kg/m^3, while steam is well under 1 kg/m^3. Liquids sit next to solids, nowhere near gases.
items.random_wrong: It is lighter, because a little mass is lost as the water freezes.

items.q: A student is finding the density of a rectangular metal block. Which measurements are needed?
items.correct: The mass from a balance, and the length, width and height from a ruler.
items.misconception: The mass from a balance, and the length of one side from a ruler.
items.why: Adding is easier than multiplying three decimals, and the student is not checking the unit of the answer. The idea that volume is a product of three lengths has been learned as a rule rather than understood. Check the unit produced by the operation. Adding metres to metres gives metres, not metres cubed. Only multiplying three lengths gives m^3.
items.random_wrong: The mass from a balance, and the area of one face from a ruler.

items.q: A measuring cylinder holds 50 cm³ of water. A stone is lowered in and the level rises to 128 cm³. What is the volume of the stone?
items.correct: 78 cm³, the rise in the water level
items.misconception: 178 cm³, the two cylinder readings added
items.why: The final reading is the number the student has just taken and it is the largest one on view, so it is copied down without asking what part of that volume is water that was already there. Label the readings before and after and write volume of object = final reading minus starting reading. Sketch the cylinder twice so the water that was already present is visible.
items.random_wrong: 128 cm³, the final reading on the cylinder

items.q: A student measures the density of cooking oil with a measuring cylinder on a balance. Which mass is divided by the volume of oil?
items.correct: The mass of cylinder and oil minus the mass of the empty cylinder.
items.misconception: The mass of the measuring cylinder once the oil has been poured in.
items.why: The balance shows one number and the cylinder shows another, so the student pairs them without noticing that the mass reading includes the glass, which contributes no volume to the 40 cm^3. Record three quantities every time: mass of empty cylinder, mass of cylinder and liquid, volume of liquid. The mass of the liquid is always the difference between the first two.
items.random_wrong: The mass of the empty measuring cylinder before the oil is added.

items.q: Which instrument is most suitable for measuring the diameter of a copper wire about 0.4 mm across?
items.correct: A micrometer, reading to 0.01 mm.
items.misconception: Vernier callipers, since they read in mm too.
items.why: Instruments are grouped by the quantity they measure rather than by their precision, so resolution is treated as a detail rather than as the reason for choosing one over another. Quote the resolution of each instrument alongside its name, and choose the instrument whose resolution is a small fraction of the length being measured.
items.random_wrong: A millimetre rule, estimated by eye.

items.q: A sealed container holds 200 g of ice. The container is left until all the ice has melted. What does the balance read now?
items.correct: 200 g, because melting rearranges the particles but removes none.
items.misconception: Less than 200 g, because some of the ice gets used up as it melts.
items.why: The everyday phrase boiled dry and the invisibility of water vapour make it look as though the water has ceased to exist. Conservation of mass is easy to state and hard to believe when the product cannot be seen. Repeat the change in a sealed container on a balance. The reading does not move, which shows the mass is still present and only its location changed in the open pan.
items.random_wrong: More than 200 g, since liquid water is denser than solid ice.

items.q: Solid carbon dioxide sublimates in an open dish on a balance and the reading falls to zero. Has any mass been destroyed?
items.correct: No, the gas has spread into the room and is not on the balance.
items.misconception: Yes, subliming uses the solid up, so that mass has gone for good now.
items.why: The everyday phrase boiled dry and the invisibility of water vapour make it look as though the water has ceased to exist. Conservation of mass is easy to state and hard to believe when the product cannot be seen. Repeat the change in a sealed container on a balance. The reading does not move, which shows the mass is still present and only its location changed in the open pan.
items.random_wrong: No, but gases weigh nothing at all, so the reading had to fall away.

items.q: Why is boiling water classed as a physical change rather than a chemical change?
items.correct: The steam is still water; cooling gives the liquid back.
items.misconception: Steam is a new substance, but a very easy one to turn back.
items.why: New appearance is taken as evidence of a new substance. A change of state alters every property a student can observe directly, so it is easy to conclude that the material itself is different. Apply the reversal test. Cool the steam and the original liquid comes back unchanged, which shows no new substance was ever made.
items.random_wrong: Physical changes are reversible and chemical changes are not.

items.q: A large block of expanded polystyrene has a greater mass than a small steel ball bearing. Which has the greater density?
items.correct: The steel. Density is mass per unit volume, not mass by itself. Steel packs about 7800 kg into each cubic metre; expanded polystyrene packs only about 20 kg into the same volume.
items.misconception: The polystyrene, because it is the heavier object, and the heavier object must be the denser one.
items.why: In everyday speech heavy and dense are used as if they meant the same thing, and students meet mass long before they meet density. Comparing objects of very different sizes hides the fact that density is a ratio, so only the top of the ratio is noticed. Insist on comparing equal volumes. Ask which is heavier, one cubic centimetre of steel or one cubic centimetre of polystyrene. Once the volume is fixed, comparing mass is comparing density.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: A balance reads 250 g. What is that mass in kilograms?
items.correct: 0.25 kg, found by dividing the reading by 1000.
items.misconception: It stays as 250 - only the label after the number changes when you rewrite it in kilograms.
items.why: Unit conversion is treated as relabelling rather than rescaling, especially when the student is copying the number straight into a calculator and thinking about the physics rather than the arithmetic. Anchor the size of the unit: a kilogram is a thousand times bigger than a gram, so the number of kilograms must be a thousand times smaller. 250 g is a quarter of a kilogram, so 0.25 kg is sensible.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Why does a substance take up more room as a gas than as a liquid?
items.correct: The particles move much further apart. The particles themselves are unchanged in size and mass.
items.misconception: The particles themselves swell up when they are heated, and that is why the gas fills a bigger space.
items.why: Expansion is an observed fact about the material, and the simplest picture of it is that everything in the material gets bigger, including the particles. Diagrams that draw gas particles larger than solid particles reinforce this. Draw all three states with identical circles and change only the spacing. Point out that the mass of each particle is fixed, so only the spacing can change the density.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Ice floats on water. What does that tell you about the density of ice?
items.correct: It is lower than the density of liquid water, because the molecules in ice are held in an open arrangement that spaces them slightly further apart.
items.misconception: When ice melts the balance reading is thought to change with the water's density or volume - judging the denser water to weigh more, or its smaller volume to weigh less - instead of mass being conserved.
items.why: The general rule that solids are denser than liquids is true for most substances and is taught as if it had no exceptions, so the floating of ice is either not noticed or explained away. Use the general rule but state the exception explicitly, with the numbers: ice is about 920 kg/m^3 against 1000 kg/m^3 for water, which is why it floats.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Which instrument should be used to measure the diameter of a wire about 0.4 mm across?
items.correct: A micrometer, because it resolves to about 0.01 mm, which is small compared with 0.4 mm.
items.misconception: A millimetre rule is fine, because you can see the wire and estimate the fraction of a millimetre between the marks.
items.why: A rule is the familiar instrument and estimating between marks feels reasonable. The student does not compare the resolution of the instrument with the size of the thing being measured. Compare resolution with measurement. A rule reading to 1 mm gives an uncertainty of more than the whole diameter; a micrometer reading to 0.01 mm gives an uncertainty of a few per cent.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: A dish of solid carbon dioxide sublimes in the open and the balance reading falls to zero. Has mass been lost from the universe?
items.correct: No. The carbon dioxide gas has spread into the room. Gases do have mass; a cubic metre of air has a mass of about 1.2 kg.
items.misconception: Gases have no mass at all, so once the solid has become a gas there is nothing left to weigh.
items.why: Gases cannot be seen, felt or held, and everyday experience offers no sense of their weight, so students treat them as nothing rather than as matter that is thinly spread. Give gases a mass in numbers: the air in a small bedroom has a mass of around 40 kg. Then weigh a sealed flask before and after air is pumped out.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: What makes a change of state a physical change rather than a chemical one?
items.correct: No new substance is formed, and reversing the change returns the material to its original properties.
items.misconception: Physical changes are simply the reversible ones, and a chemical change can never be reversed.
items.why: Reversibility is a useful signpost and gets promoted into the definition, even though many chemical changes, such as the reaction of hydrogen and oxygen, can be reversed by other means. Define the difference by what is present afterwards: a physical change leaves the same substance, a chemical change makes new ones. Reversibility is then a consequence, not the test itself.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Which unit does the AQA specification use for density in the equation rho = m/V?
items.correct: Kilograms per metre cubed, kg/m³, because the specification uses mass in kilograms and volume in metres cubed.
items.misconception: Density is measured in grams per centimetre cubed, g/cm³ - that is the density unit, because it is the one always used in lessons and data tables.
items.why: Classroom practicals and chemistry data tables almost always quote densities in g/cm³, because blocks and liquids are measured in grams and centimetres, so students take the familiar unit to be the standard one. g/cm³ is a valid everyday unit, but the specification's standard unit is kg/m³, built from the SI units kilogram and metre. Values can be converted: 1 g/cm³ = 1000 kg/m³, so water is 1 g/cm³ or 1000 kg/m³.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented
